The effects are likely correlation, not causation. Also, bigger is not necessarily better. In domestication we selectively breed to produce more desirable traits, but there are limits just as in natural selection. Having a large head (and thereby brain mass) relative to body size can actually be detrimental. A larger skull is needed to protect the brain, which requires food and energy to grow and may not have as strong of survival benefits. A larger head can also make birthing more difficult, and increase the likelihood of death for both the mother and the child.

Bigger brains also don't necessarily equate to more intelligence. In the case of Homo neanderthalensis the larger brain size was relative to body size and makes sense due to the colder climate in which they lived when compared to early Homo sapiens. Neanderthals were, generally speaking, more robust in body size with shorter, stockier limbs that were more efficient for conservation of heat. As such they also had more musculature than Homo sapiens. In regards to brain function: it's not so much the size, but how you use it. Neanderthals had a larger visual cortex than humans, but human's have a larger parietal lobe. Portions of the parietal lobe contribute to language development, and a difference in the FOXP2 gene between humans and neanderthals further support the idea that humans developed a brain that functioned differently than a neanderthal's. Neanderthals evidenced some precursors to symbolic language and behavior, such as cave paintings, ornamentation, and crude burial of the dead, but they did not develop language the same way human's did. Arguably, human language is one of our greatest evolutionary strengths.

Would you not agree that on average a larger brain is likely to have greater capabilities than a smaller brain? Would it not be absurd to claim that smaller brains would normally have greater capabilities Qthan larger brains?

Of course there are a variety of issues involved, but many of the "Does not necessarily" claims that are evoked defy the tests of reasonableness and at a minimum the expectations of Occam's razor.
